2 Timothy 1.summary: Paul, identifying himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, writes to Timothy, whom he calls his beloved child (2 Timothy 1:1-2). He thanks God as he remembers Timothy constantly in prayer, recalls Timothy's tears, and longs to see him (2 Timothy 1:3-4). He recalls Timothy's sincere faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Paul urges Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God that is in him through the laying on of Paul's hands, because God gave a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control (2 Timothy 1:6-7). Timothy is not to be ashamed of the testimony about the Lord or of Paul, the Lord's prisoner, but to share in suffering for the gospel by God's power (2 Timothy 1:8). Paul describes God as the one who saved and called believers, not because of works but by his own purpose and grace, now made known through the appearing of Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light (2 Timothy 1:9-10). Paul was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher of this gospel; he suffers for it but is not ashamed, because he knows whom he has believed (2 Timothy 1:11-12). Timothy is to hold to the pattern of sound words and guard the good deposit by the Holy Spirit (2 Timothy 1:13-14). Paul notes that all who are in Asia turned away from him, naming Phygelus and Hermogenes (2 Timothy 1:15), and contrasts them with Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains (2 Timothy 1:16-18).
2 Timothy 1.whereWeAre:
Paul is a prisoner, in chains, and Onesiphorus had to search for him in Rome and find him (1:8, 1:16-17).

Timothy appears elsewhere in Scripture as a younger co-worker of Paul, the son of a Jewish believing mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1-3), and as Paul's representative in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3).

'Asia' was a Roman province in western Asia Minor with Ephesus as an important city (Acts 19:10 says all the residents of Asia heard the word).

In the ancient world prisoners often depended on friends and family for food and care. A second-century satirist, Lucian, mocks but describes Christians bringing food and care to the imprisoned Peregrinus, then a Christian leader (The Passing of Peregrinus 12-13), which illustrates how a visitor like Onesiphorus could be of real help.

Whether this imprisonment was the same as the one at the end of Acts or a later one is disputed. Early Christian tradition speaks of release and a later second arrest (Eusebius, Church History 2.22), but this is not stated in Scripture. The letter's opening shows Paul in suffering and in need of loyal friends, and shows Timothy as a younger leader who may be tempted to be ashamed. The call to endure and guard the gospel makes best sense against Paul's imprisonment and the desertion he describes.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Writes to encourage Timothy, recalls his own appointment as preacher and apostle and teacher, and reports who stood by him and who did not. His example of suffering without shame shapes the charge to Timothy.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Urged to rekindle his gift, not be ashamed, share in suffering, follow sound words and guard the deposit. The one entrusted in the letter with guarding the gospel and passing it on.

keyFigures.name: Lois and Eunice
keyFigures.role: Paul remembers that the sincere faith dwelling in Timothy lived first in them. They show faith handed on within a family.

keyFigures.name: Phygelus and Hermogenes
keyFigures.role: Named as examples of desertion. Nothing else is recorded about them in Scripture; further details are unknown.

keyFigures.name: Onesiphorus
keyFigures.role: Often refreshed Paul, was not ashamed of his chains, and sought him out in Rome. Serves as a contrast to those who turned away.

keyFigures.name: Those in Asia
keyFigures.role: Described as having turned away from Paul. Their abandonment fits the loneliness and pressure of Paul's situation, though the text gives no reasons.

keyFigures.name: God and Christ Jesus
keyFigures.role: God gave the Spirit of power, love and self-control, saved and called believers by his grace; Christ Jesus abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. The saving work of God in Christ is the basis for Paul's confidence.

keyFigures.name: Nero
keyFigures.role: Not mentioned in the chapter. Supplies the political background if Paul wrote from a Roman imprisonment in the 60s AD.

keyThemes.theme: Courage in the face of shame and suffering
keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy is told not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of Paul the prisoner, but to share in suffering by God's power. Paul says he himself is not ashamed.

The letter links courage to the gift of God's Spirit of power, love and self-control and not to personal temperament.

keyThemes.theme: Salvation by God's grace and purpose
keyThemes.explanation:
God saved and called believers not because of works but by his own purpose and grace given before the ages began and revealed in Christ.

The passage presents salvation as God's initiative and gift.

keyThemes.theme: Guarding and handing on the gospel
keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy is to follow the pattern of sound words and guard the good deposit by the Holy Spirit.

Faithful teaching is presented as a responsibility shared with the Spirit's help.

keyThemes.theme: Rekindling a gift and a heritage of faith
keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy's faith is traced to Lois and Eunice, and he is urged to fan his gift into flame.

The passage encourages readers to value those who handed faith to them and to keep it active.

All who are in Asia turned away from Paul, while Onesiphorus stood by him.

The chapter holds up practical, costly support for fellow believers as worthy of honor.

2 Timothy 2.summary: Paul tells Timothy to be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus and to entrust what he has heard from Paul to faithful people who will be able to teach others (2 Timothy 2:1-2). He urges Timothy to share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus, comparing the Christian worker to a soldier who avoids civilian entanglements, an athlete who competes by the rules, and a hard-working farmer who should have the first share of the crops (2 Timothy 2:3-6). He tells Timothy to think about these things and promises that the Lord will give understanding (2 Timothy 2:7). Timothy is to remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, a descendant of David, which is Paul's gospel and the reason for his suffering, though the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:8-9). Paul endures everything for the sake of the elect so that they may obtain salvation and eternal glory (2 Timothy 2:10). He quotes a trustworthy saying about dying and living with Christ, enduring and reigning, denying and being denied, and being faithless while Christ remains faithful (2 Timothy 2:11-13). Timothy is to remind believers to avoid quarreling about words, to be a worker who has no need to be ashamed and rightly handles the word of truth, and to avoid irreverent babble that spreads like gangrene, as with Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened (2 Timothy 2:14-18). God's firm foundation stands with the seal 'The Lord knows those who are his' and 'Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity' (2 Timothy 2:19). In a great house there are vessels for honorable and dishonorable use, and whoever cleanses himself will be a vessel for honorable use (2 Timothy 2:20-21). Timothy is to flee youthful passions, pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart, and avoid foolish controversies (2 Timothy 2:22-23). The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind, able to teach and patiently enduring evil, correcting opponents with gentleness in the hope that God may grant them repentance and that they may escape the snare of the devil (2 Timothy 2:24-26).
2 Timothy 2.whereWeAre:
Paul is suffering and chained 'like a criminal' for the gospel, but the word of God is not bound (2:9).

Roman soldiers were professionals whose service required devotion to their commander and avoidance of other business; the image appears elsewhere in Paul's letters, where he calls Epaphroditus and Archippus 'fellow soldier' (Philippians 2:25; Philemon 1:2).

Greek athletic contests, such as the Isthmian Games near Corinth, had strict rules, and winners were crowned with a wreath (compare 1 Corinthians 9:24-25).

Farming was the basis of the economy in the Roman world.

Hymenaeus and Philetus held a teaching about resurrection that the letter condemns; the details of their teaching are not given in the text. The images, the saying and the references to false teaching describe the challenges Timothy faced and how he was to respond. They show that the early church faced opposition from outside and confusion from within.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Addressed throughout and given the charge to be strong, entrust the teaching to faithful people, endure suffering, and correct opponents gently. His faithfulness is central to the continuation of the gospel in the letter.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Teaches Timothy, describes his own suffering, and endures for the elect. His example of endurance supports the charge to Timothy.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: He is the center of Paul's gospel and the one who remains faithful (2:13). The gospel and the hope of the chapter depend on him.

keyFigures.name: Faithful people who will teach others
keyFigures.role: Receive what Timothy has heard from Paul and teach others. Show the intended chain of handing on the gospel in four stages: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, others.

keyFigures.name: The elect
keyFigures.role: Receive salvation in Christ Jesus with eternal glory. Paul's endurance is aimed at their benefit.

keyFigures.name: Hymenaeus and Philetus
keyFigures.role: They say the resurrection has already happened and upset the faith of some. They serve as examples of harmful teaching. Hymenaeus is also named in 1 Timothy 1:20; nothing else is known of Philetus.

keyFigures.name: The Lord's servant
keyFigures.role: Is kind, able to teach and patient, correcting opponents with gentleness. Sets the manner of ministry the chapter commends.

keyFigures.name: Opponents
keyFigures.role: They are to be corrected gently in the hope of repentance. The passage presents them as people who may yet come to the truth.

keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy is to entrust what he has heard from Paul to faithful people who will teach others, and to rightly handle the word of truth.

Faithful teaching is presented as a task shared by many people and not only a leader.

Soldier, athlete and farmer are used to illustrate perseverance; Paul endures for the sake of the elect.

The chapter links endurance with hope in the reward and in Christ's faithfulness.

The saying ends with the statement that if we are faithless he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.

The passage invites readers to trust Christ's faithfulness while taking his call seriously.

keyThemes.theme: Guarding against destructive talk and false teaching
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to avoid quarrels about words, irreverent babble and teaching like that of Hymenaeus and Philetus.

The chapter encourages discernment about teaching.

Timothy is to cleanse himself, flee youthful passions, pursue righteousness, and correct opponents gently.

Firm commitment to truth is joined with patience toward opponents.

2 Timothy 3.summary: Paul warns Timothy that in the last days there will be times of difficulty, when people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power; Timothy is to avoid such people (2 Timothy 3:1-5). Among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women burdened with sins and led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 3:6-7). As Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, these people oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith; but they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all (2 Timothy 3:8-9). In contrast, Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, conduct, aim, faith, patience, love, steadfastness, persecutions and sufferings, including those at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, from which the Lord rescued Paul (2 Timothy 3:10-11). Paul says that all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived (2 Timothy 3:12-13). Timothy is to continue in what he has learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom he learned it and that from childhood he has been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 3:14-15). All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction and training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17).
2 Timothy 3.whereWeAre:
Paul was driven out of Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:50), fled Iconium when a plot to mistreat and stone him came to light (14:5-6), and was stoned at Lystra, after which he got up and left the next day (14:19-20). Timothy was a disciple at Lystra, well spoken of by the believers at Lystra and Iconium (Acts 16:1-2).

Timothy grew up with knowledge of 'the sacred writings' (3:15), which in the first century were the Jewish Scriptures; his mother and grandmother are named in 1:5 and Acts 16:1 says his mother was a Jewish believer.

Jewish writings speak of Jannes and Jambres as magicians or opponents of Moses; the Damascus Document (probably second to first century BC) is among the earliest surviving texts to name them, but their relation to Paul's source is unknown.

Greek and Roman writers often used lists of vices, and similar lists appear in Romans 1:29-31 and Galatians 5:19-21, which suggests a common way of describing moral failings.

Christians in Rome were being persecuted under Nero after the fire of AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Whether this affected Paul's imprisonment is not stated in Scripture. The mention of earlier persecution, the comparison to Moses' opponents and the emphasis on Scripture anchor Paul's warning in real history and in the Jewish Scriptures that shaped Timothy. They show that opposition to God's messengers was a long-standing pattern and that Timothy had a firm foundation.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Warned about difficult times, urged to avoid certain people, reminded of Paul's example and of the Scriptures he has known from childhood. The chapter's instructions apply to his ministry.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Provides an example for Timothy to follow. His life is offered as evidence that faithful living brings persecution and also the Lord's deliverance.

keyFigures.name: People of the last days
keyFigures.role: Described as having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. They represent the danger Timothy must avoid.

keyFigures.name: Those who creep into households and the women they capture
keyFigures.role: Described as taking advantage of weak women burdened with sins and passions. Show how false teaching can spread within households.

keyFigures.name: Jannes and Jambres
keyFigures.role: Paul compares the false teachers to them. Their names illustrate the long history of opposition to God's truth. The details come from tradition, not Scripture.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Named as the one opposed. Provides the pattern of opposition to God's messenger.

keyFigures.name: Persecutors and evil people and impostors
keyFigures.role: They persecute believers or deceive and are deceived. Their presence shows the cost of godliness.

keyFigures.name: The Lord
keyFigures.role: Rescued Paul out of all his persecutions. He is the source of deliverance.

keyThemes.explanation:
Paul lists vices and says some have the appearance of godliness but deny its power; Timothy is to avoid them.

The chapter invites readers to test faith by its fruit and not only by its appearance.

Paul reminds Timothy of the persecutions he endured and says all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.

The passage invites readers to expect opposition without presenting it as a sign of failure.

keyThemes.theme: Following a model of faithful living
keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, conduct and endurance and is to continue in what he has learned.

The chapter values both teaching and example.

The sacred writings are able to make one wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and all Scripture is God-breathed and profitable.

Readers are directed to Scripture as the foundation for teaching and for growth.

The opponents will not get far because their folly will be plain.

The passage is both a warning and an encouragement.

2 Timothy 4.summary: Paul solemnly charges Timothy in the presence of God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word, be ready in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching (2 Timothy 4:1-2). A time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching but, having itching ears, will accumulate teachers to suit their own passions and wander off into myths (2 Timothy 4:3-4). Timothy is to be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist and fulfill his ministry (2 Timothy 4:5). Paul says he is already being poured out as a drink offering and the time of his departure has come; he has fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith, and the crown of righteousness is laid up for him and for all who have loved the Lord's appearing (2 Timothy 4:6-8). He asks Timothy to come soon, reports that Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted him, that Crescens has gone to Galatia and Titus to Dalmatia, that he has sent Tychicus to Ephesus, and that only Luke is with him; he asks Timothy to bring Mark, his cloak, the books and above all the parchments (2 Timothy 4:9-13). He warns about Alexander the coppersmith, who did him great harm (2 Timothy 4:14-15). At his first defense no one stood by him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him, and he was rescued from the lion's mouth (2 Timothy 4:16-17). He is confident that the Lord will rescue him from every evil deed and bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom (2 Timothy 4:18). He sends greetings to Prisca, Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus, mentions Erastus and Trophimus, urges Timothy to come before winter, passes on greetings from Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brothers, and closes with a blessing (2 Timothy 4:19-22).
2 Timothy 4.whereWeAre:
Paul is awaiting the outcome of a legal process and says he has already made a first defense (4:16).

Paul's co-workers are scattered across the Mediterranean: Thessalonica, Galatia (or Gaul), Dalmatia, Ephesus, Troas, Corinth and Miletus (4:10-13, 4:20).

Early Christian tradition reports that Paul was martyred (1 Clement 5, which does not name Rome) and, in Eusebius, that he was put to death in Rome under Nero (Church History 2.22, 2.25). The letter itself does not record his death.

Sailing in the Mediterranean was dangerous in the winter (compare Acts 27:9-12), which is relevant to Paul's request to come 'before winter' (4:21).

Under Nero, Christians in Rome were punished following the fire of AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). How this relates to Paul's trial is not stated. The final chapter shows Paul at the end of his life: isolated, but confident, passing the work on to Timothy. The practical details, such as the cloak, the travel and the greetings, show the real circumstances behind the charge.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Gives his final charge, speaks of his coming departure, asks for Timothy and for items, and reports abandonment and rescue. The chapter functions as his testament.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Charged to preach the word, endure, bring Mark and the cloak, beware of Alexander, and come before winter. The chapter hands the work on to him.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ and God
keyFigures.role: Judge of the living and the dead; Lord who stood by Paul and will rescue him. The charge and Paul's hope rest on him.

keyFigures.name: Demas
keyFigures.role: In love with this present world, deserted Paul and went to Thessalonica. A sad contrast to Luke and others.

keyFigures.name: Crescens, Titus and Tychicus
keyFigures.role: Crescens went to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia, and Tychicus was sent to Ephesus. Show Paul's wide network of co-workers.

keyFigures.name: Luke
keyFigures.role: Alone with Paul. Paul notes that he alone remains with him.

keyFigures.name: Mark
keyFigures.role: Timothy is to bring him because he is useful for ministry. Paul calls him useful for ministry, which contrasts with the earlier disagreement over him (Acts 15:37-39); the text does not say more about their relationship.

keyFigures.name: Carpus
keyFigures.role: Holds the cloak, books and parchments. Otherwise unknown.

keyFigures.name: Alexander the coppersmith
keyFigures.role: Paul warns Timothy to beware of him. Otherwise unknown from this passage; whether he is the Alexander of 1 Timothy 1:20 is not stated.

keyFigures.name: Prisca and Aquila
keyFigures.role: Greeted by Paul. Part of Paul's circle of friends.

keyFigures.name: Household of Onesiphorus
keyFigures.role: Greeted by Paul. Links to chapter 1.

keyFigures.name: Erastus and Trophimus
keyFigures.role: Mentioned in Paul's travel report. Part of Paul's report on where his co-workers were; the text does not say why Trophimus was left ill.

keyFigures.name: Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brothers
keyFigures.role: Send greetings to Timothy. Show the believers around Paul, presumably in Rome. Nothing further is stated about them.

keyThemes.explanation:
Timothy is charged to preach the word in all circumstances.

Faithful teaching is presented as the task of the minister.

keyThemes.theme: Resisting teachers who say what people want to hear
keyThemes.explanation:
People will not listen to sound teaching but will accumulate teachers to suit their own passions, turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.

The chapter encourages readers to value truth over comfort.

Paul looks back on his course, saying he fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith.

Readers are invited to see perseverance as the goal.

Demas deserted Paul, others left, and no one stood by him at his defense, while Luke and others remained.

The chapter treats loyalty as a gift and desertion as a sorrow.

The Lord stood by Paul and strengthened him and will bring him safely to his heavenly kingdom.

The passage points to the Lord's presence in hardship.
